title: Som Tum
subtitle: thai green papaya salad using courgette
excerpt: Shredded courgette pounded with lime, fish sauce, chilli, palm sugar, and tomatoes to make the iconic Thai salad. Sharp, salty, hot, and sweet in every bite. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Som tum originates in northeastern Thailand (Isaan) and Laos. The traditional version uses green papaya. This version uses courgette as a widely available substitute with a similar texture when uncooked.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Dress the salad no more than 30 minutes before eating. The courgette softens quickly after dressing.

glossaryTerms.definition: The technique used to make som tum. Ingredients are bruised and crushed in a mortar rather than mixed. Pounding breaks down the fibres and allows the dressing to penetrate deeply into the salad without turning it into a paste.

The Thai principle of balancing sour, salty, sweet, and hot in every dish. In som tum, lime provides sour, fish sauce provides salt, palm sugar provides sweet, and chilli provides heat. All four must be present and in balance.
A salty, pungent condiment made from fermented fish, used across Southeast Asian cooking as a primary salt source. In Thai cooking it is never cooked; it is added raw to preserve its freshness.

content.text: technique. A large pestle and mortar is essential. The courgette must be pounded to bruise it but not reduce it to mush. Each pound should leave the strands intact but softened and permeated with dressing.

content.text: Shred the courgette into thin matchsticks using a julienne peeler or the julienne setting on a box grater. Spread on a clean cloth and press firmly to squeeze out as much moisture as possible.
Place the garlic and chillies in the mortar. Pound until broken down but not a paste. Add the dried chillies if using and pound briefly.
Add the sugar and pound to dissolve. Add the lime juice, fish sauce, and tamarind if using. Stir to combine the dressing in the mortar.
Add the green beans and pound 3 to 4 times to bruise them. Add the tomatoes and pound 2 to 3 times more.
Add the shredded courgette in 2 batches. Pound and toss each batch into the dressing, turning it over with a spoon between pounds.
Taste and adjust. More lime for sour, more fish sauce for salt, more sugar for sweet, more chilli for heat. Transfer to a plate. Scatter the crushed peanuts over the top. Eat immediately.

attrs.cause: The courgette was not squeezed dry before pounding, releasing its water into the dressing.
attrs.fix: Always press the courgette firmly before use. If the salad is already watery, drain off the excess liquid and taste before adding more dressing.

attrs.symptom: Dressing tastes flat despite having all four flavours
attrs.cause: The garlic and chilli were not pounded well enough, so they did not integrate into the dressing.
attrs.fix: Pound the garlic and chilli very thoroughly at the start. They should be almost entirely dissolved before any liquid goes in.

content.text: Som tum is native to northeastern Thailand and Laos and is the most popular dish in Isaan, a large agricultural region that provides much of Thailand's rice and is home to a distinct food culture. It was considered a regional working-class food until the 1980s, when internal migration brought Isaan cooks to Bangkok. Street food stalls selling som tum became common across the capital and then spread throughout Thailand. It is now eaten at every level of Thai society and across the Thai diaspora worldwide.
